item.title: Batam Fast Sails to Desaru Too, but Only Thursday to Monday
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
A weekend getaway to Desaru in Malaysia sounds relaxing, but getting there from Singapore means dealing with busy land checkpoints and unpredictable road traffic. For travelers who prefer to skip the drive, the Batam Fast ferry offers another way to reach Johor's coastal resort area. The ferry connects Tanah Merah Ferry Terminal with Desaru Coast in approximately 90 minutes. Its published schedule shows services from Thursday to Monday, making it an option for short breaks and weekend trips. However, limited departures mean timing matters. Before booking, understand the ferry schedule, ticket prices, immigration requirements, and how much time you can realistically spend in Desaru. Batam Fast Runs a Ferry to Desaru From Thursday to Monday The Singapore to Desaru Ferry connects Singapore with Desaru Coast in Johor, letting you reach the resort area without driving across the land border. Batam Fast operates the route, with the published schedule covering Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday and Monday. This gives you more flexibility than a Thursday-to-Sunday schedule suggests, but the service does not run every day. If your preferred travel date falls outside the published days, check the booking calendar or consider traveling by road. Treat the timetable as the starting point for your plans. The operator notes that schedules and routes may change, so confirm departure and return times for your chosen date before booking accommodation. The Timetable: 10:10 am Out, 5:30 pm Back The published schedule lists an outbound departure from Tanah Merah around 10:10 am and a return from Desaru Coast around 5:30 pm. The crossing takes about 90 minutes, though the actual schedule and experience can vary. One-way Batam Fast ferry tickets from Singapore to Desaru Coast start from about S$70 per adult, based on the available route listing. Check the fare for your travel date and review any additional charges before booking. Do not rely on these times as a guarantee for every date. Check the booking calendar and the operator's latest timetable, and ensure the return sailing is available before finalizing your plans. With limited departures, missing your ferry could affect your trip. Ferry or Causeway: When the 90-Minute Crossing Makes Sense You can also reach Desaru by road. Driving gives you more flexibility to explore different parts of Johor, travel outside the ferry's operating days, or continue beyond the resort area. However, the journey entails road travel and land-border formalities, and traffic can add time on weekends and holidays. The Batam Fast Ferry is worth considering if you're heading straight to Desaru Coast and prefer not to drive. The crossing takes about 90 minutes and avoids the land border crossing. You will still need to complete ferry check-in and immigration procedures. The best option depends on your plans. Choose the ferry if its timetable fits your dates and your destination is convenient from Desaru Coast Ferry Terminal. Driving may be more practical if you need flexible departure times or want to visit several places on the same trip. Arriving in Malaysia by Sea: Passport and MDAC Requirements Desaru is in Malaysia, so the ferry trip involves an international border crossing. Bring a valid passport and complete the required immigration procedures at departure and arrival. Many foreign visitors who are not exempt must submit the Malaysia Digital Arrival Card (MDAC) within the three days before arriving in Malaysia. However, exemptions remain, including for Singapore citizens. Check the current Malaysian immigration requirements for your nationality before traveling rather than assuming that everyone needs to submit the form. If you need to complete the MDAC, use the official Malaysian immigration website and submit it within the permitted window. Keep your passport and ferry booking details accessible at the terminal, and follow the operator's instructions for check-in and immigration. Malaysia and Singapore use the same time zone, so you do not need to adjust your watch when you arrive in Desaru. Day Trip or Overnight: What Fits Between the Sailings? The listed 10:10 am outbound and 5:30 pm return departures can make a day trip possible, depending on your sailing schedule. However, the time between sailings is not all free time. Allow time for check-in, immigration, travel to and from attractions, and returning to the terminal. For a short visit, choose one main activity or a nearby beach and allow enough time to return for your ferry. Check opening hours and transfer arrangements before deciding what to fit into the day. An overnight stay is more relaxed if you want to enjoy the resorts, waterpark, golf, or other attractions without watching the clock. Before booking a hotel, check the next day's return ferry schedule and make sure the service runs on your intended return date. Tanah Merah Ferry Terminal is in eastern Singapore, so plan your transit before departure day. Public transport is an option, but check the latest MRT and bus information for your travel date rather than relying on a fixed journey time. A taxi or ride-hailing service may be more convenient if you have luggage or are traveling in a group. Journey times depend on your starting point and traffic conditions. Follow the ferry operator's check-in deadline and allow enough time to reach the terminal, check in, and clear immigration. Because departures are limited, arriving late could mean missing your sailing. The Singapore to Desaru ferry is a useful alternative to driving if the Batam Fast schedule fits your plans. The published timetable covers Thursday to Monday, with an outbound sailing around 10:10 am and a return around 5:30 pm. Check current times and availability before booking, as the operator may change its schedule. Carry your passport, check whether you need to submit the MDAC, and allow enough time for check-in and immigration. A day trip works if you plan one or two nearby activities, while an overnight stay gives you more time to enjoy Desaru Coast without rushing to catch the ferry. Does Batam Fast sail from Singapore to Desaru? Yes. Batam Fast operates a direct ferry service from Tanah Merah Ferry Terminal to Desaru Coast Ferry Terminal. Its published schedule covers Thursday to Monday, but check the current timetable for your travel date. What are the sailing times? The published schedule lists an outbound departure at around 10:10 am and a return departure at around 5:30 pm. Verify both times when booking because schedules can change. How long is the crossing, and is it faster than driving? The ferry crossing takes about 90 minutes. Driving time depends on your starting point, route, and land-border traffic, so compare the full trip rather than assuming one option will always be faster. Do I need a passport and the MDAC? You need a valid passport for the international journey. Many foreign visitors who are not exempt must submit the Malaysia Digital Arrival Card within the three days before arrival, but exemptions apply. Check the current rules for your nationality. Can I do Desaru as a day trip by ferry? A day trip may be possible with the listed sailing times, but you'll have limited time at your destination once check-in, immigration, and transfers are included. An overnight stay gives you more flexibility. This story was published in partnership with redBus.

item.title: IDEA: Forget the Florida Trail, These 6 Hikes Reveal The Wild Variety of The Sunshine State
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Florida may be best known for its beaches, theme parks, and sprawling wetlands, but if you are willing to venture inland, you will find a surprisingly diverse set of hikes in an equally varied landscape. Trails along sandy ridges, shady hardwood hammocks that shelter wildlife, and deep ravines providing a welcome escape from the subtropical heat are scattered across the state. And you don’t even have to commit to a months-long thru-hike to experience them. From ancient dunes to forested ravines, these six all-season, pet-friendly trails offer a reason to lace up your hiking boots and explore the wilder side of the Sunshine State. They are open from dawn to dusk, and some even allow camping for a small fee if you want to make your hike an overnight trip. Entrance fee: $5 per vehicle, $2 for pedestrians and bicycles. >Highlight: The trail is especially beautiful during azalea season, from late January through March, when the park’s flowering shrubs explode in splashes of pink, red, and white. This part of Florida is unlike anything you’ll find along the coast, with steep paths covered with ancient root systems of Azalea bushes. The 2.5-mile Azalea Trail at Ravine Gardens State Park is a short but challenging loop that takes hikers along narrow dirt paths, over exposed roots, and down historic stone staircases. There are two suspension bridges over a spring-fed creek that flows through a shaded forest of ferns, mosses, and native trees. Entrance fee: $6 per vehicle, $5 camping permit per night. >Camping: Three campgrounds with 90 sites with water and electric hookups (check water conditions before camping) and six primitive campgrounds with three sites each Highlight: You may spot wild turkeys and alligators, so be sure to stay on the trail at all times, especially through the open prairies. Myakka River State Park, just east of Sarasota, is one of Florida’s largest and most ecologically diverse state parks. The Myakka trail is a roughly 39-mile loop. It winds through pine flatwoods, oak and palm hammocks, open prairie, and wetlands. Several shorter day hikes like the 5.4-mile Bee Island and 8.7-mile Honore branch out from the main trail. Those are great alternatives if you don’t want to stay overnight. Location: 13201 San Felasco Parkway, Alachua Entrance fee: $4 per vehicle, $2 for pedestrians and bicycles; dogs are not allowed in some sections frequented by birders. >Highlight: Birding is very popular here as species like the Wood Thrush and Red-headed woodpecker thrive in the park’s varied ecosystems. The San Felasco Hammock Preserve State Park is home to one of the only remaining hardwood forests in Florida. The Spring Grove Trail is a 5.8-mile loop that passes through a variety of habitats and ecosystems within the park and is a great reminder that Florida’s natural diversity isn’t limited to its famous swamps and coastlines. This trail passes through shady hardwood hammocks, pine forests, and sandy hills. There are also both dry and water-filled sinkholes, adding interesting terrain features along the way. You can also hike a shorter 2.8-mile loop up to the Hammock cutoff. Entrance fee: None. Highlight: Explore a swampy jungle that is teeming with Florida wildlife of all shapes and sizes. If you’re looking for that classic, marshland, jungle Florida experience, with rugged hiking and tons of wildlife, look no further than the Black Bear Wilderness Area. This 7.1-mile loop trail takes you deep into lowland habitats like wet prairie, hydric hammock, and cypress swamp. The trail is challenging in spots, due to roots, boulders, and muddy sections. Bugs and humidity are to be expected, but it’s worth putting up with those for the chance to see some wildlife. Hikers often encounter river otters, alligators, white-tailed deer, tons of bird life, and, if it’s quiet enough, even black bears. Location: 4335 Firetower Road, Haines City Entrance fee: Free; $5 camping permit per night. >Highlight: It is home to 21 rare plants and 31 animals, some of which are not found anywhere else in the world. You might see scrub morning glory, pygmy fringe tree, and cutthroat grass, along with protected animal species including the Florida scrub-jay and gopher tortoise. The Allen David Broussard Catfish Creek Preserve State Park is located along the Lake Wales Ridge. It includes Florida’s most unusual ecosystems—an ancient shoreline and sandbar dating back almost 350,000 years. The park protects more than 8,000 acres of scrub, sandhill, and flatwoods habitat. The Catfish Creek Trail is a 5.8-mile loop that is mostly exposed with little to no shade. This trail crosses a lot of sandy terrain, which can make even a relatively short walk feel strenuous. Be prepared with plenty of water and consider bringing your own shade. Location: Torreya State Park Loop Parking Lot, Bristol Entrance fee: $3 vehicle entrance fee; $5 backcountry camping fee Highlight: Striking cliff formation and primitive camping for backpackers. This hike follows the Apalachicola River and offers some of the most challenging terrain in this part of Florida. It can be completed as a 7-mile single loop if you want a shorter dayhike. Or, extend the hike by adding the second loop. It connects with the first and nearly doubles the distance to 13 miles. In total, you’ll gain a whopping 1,646 feet of elevation. If you want to make this an overnight adventure, there are three different primitive campsites along the trail. Campsites require a $5 backcountry camping fee and must be reserved at Torreya State Park or by phone at 850-643-2674.

item.title: Meet Design Hotels, Marriott's collection of one-of-a-kind hotels you can book with points
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
It's a common misconception that trendy, boutique hotels don't live in the points, miles and loyalty ecosystem. However, there are actually hundreds — and hundreds! — of incredible, independent hotels that are the opposite of cookie-cutter (think: small room counts, art-filled lobbies and a distinct sense of place). A lot of these stylish, boutique hotels enter the points world through curated hotel collections that participate in loyalty programs, giving hotels a wider reach of potential guests without having to adhere to strict brand standards that change the spirit of the property. One of the pioneers in this space is Design Hotels, a collection of hundreds of independently-owned hotels and resorts dotting the globe, each with its own identity, personality and approach to hospitality. "Every hotel is picked for its originality [and] the vision that's behind it," Stijn Oyen, managing director at Design Hotels, told TPG, adding that each property has "a strong point of view and cultural connection." And it's not necessarily easy to make the cut for this collection: According to Oyen, only about 5% of the hotels that apply to join Design Hotels are accepted in an effort to "stay true to the original roots and values of what makes a design hotel." Then there's the loyalty twist: Marriott actually owns Design Hotels, and many (but not all) of the collection's properties participate in Marriott Bonvoy. Here's a quick guide to everything you need to know about Design Hotels, plus a few standout properties where you can earn and burn Marriott Bonvoy points. What is Design Hotels? Founded in the early 1990s, Design Hotels was created to bring together independently owned, design-forward hotels that shared a commitment to originality, creativity and local culture. Today, that collection is more than 300 members strong, with new properties regularly joining. What differentiates the collection is the individuality of each property — each one has its own unique point of view, rather than a prescribed set of standards travelers will see at more traditional hotel brands. "We're set up around design," Oyen explained. "It's about the vision. It's about being independent with a voice." Design Hotels became part of Marriott's portfolio following the hotel giant's acquisition of Starwood Hotels & Resorts in 2016, giving Marriott a majority stake in the company. By 2021, Marriott had acquired full ownership of Design Hotels, though the collection continues to operate as a separate entity, with member hotels retaining their individual identities and independence. What makes a Design Hotel? The company describes its properties as "design-driven hotels that function as social hubs and spaces for purposeful experiences." But what does that actually mean? To start, getting into the collection isn't easy, and Design Hotels is looking for one distinguishing factor before choosing a new member: "the originality in its concept." According to Oyen, only about 5% of applicants pass the test. Hotels are also evaluated on everything from design and sustainability to cultural programming and the property's connection to its local community. "It's a strong, strong sense of place," Oyen explained, adding that beyond their physical design, the hotels should have vibrant public spaces that attract locals and feel like an extension of the neighborhoods they call home. It's also about the people. According to Oyen, about 60% of Design Hotels owners are first-time hoteliers, bringing fresh perspectives and new approaches to hospitality. The company calls the creative minds behind its properties "Originals," describing them as "the engines behind pioneering design and revolutionary hospitality," according to the brand's website. Without rigid brand standards dictating every detail, these hoteliers have the freedom to pursue projects that seasoned hospitality pros might consider too risky. That might be as simple as removing TVs from guest rooms or as dramatic as building a hotel accessible only by cable car, like Vigilius Mountain Resort in Italy's Dolomites. How does Design Hotels work with Marriott Bonvoy? For Marriott Bonvoy members, Design Hotels offers a truly independent, boutique-like stay while still allowing them to earn and burn points. Something that, frankly, a lot of people don't realize is available to them in the loyalty world. Just don't forget: Not all Design Hotels participate in Marriott Bonvoy. To see a full list of the 120-plus participating hotels, visit Marriott's dedicated Design Hotels landing page. For Design Hotels, according to Oyen, the relationship with Marriott is a win-win situation: Hotels gain access to nearly 300 million loyalty members while maintaining their "complete independence." But because these properties operate differently from traditional Marriott hotels, Bonvoy elite members shouldn't expect all their usual perks to apply. Here's what members can expect based on their status. The following Marriott Bonvoy benefits are excluded at Design Hotels: Set near the beach in Casablanca, Villa Sahrai pays respect to "Casablanca’s Art Deco tradition" across its 56 rooms and public spaces. Be sure to take advantage of the spa and its Moroccan hammam before settling down for food at one of two restaurants or a nightcap at the bar. How to book: Cash rates from around $160 per night or 34,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night. To get to Vigilius Mountain Resort, guests must ascend a private cable car that travels between the mountain hotel and the village it soars above. But once up at the top, guests are treated to beautiful Dolomite views, architecture that incorporates nature and wellness experiences around every stylish corner. How to book: Cash rates from about $341 per night or 47,000 Marriott Bonvoy points. At The Austin Proper Hotel, patterns, textures and colors combine in unexpected and beautiful ways from the moment guests step inside until their head hits the pillow. The hotel is as cool as Austin itself, but also full of surprises: You can grab classic Tex-Mex to eat or opt for a French Japanese tasting menu or soak up the sun at the rooftop pool before a lymphatic drain at the Verbena Spa. How to book: Cash rates from $350 or 54,000 Marriott Bonvoy points. Kyoto is no stranger to incredible hotels, but Genji Kyoto offers an intimate experience with just 20 rooms that feel distinctly Japanese and totally sleek and fresh. As serene as they come, spend a day getting lost in Kyoto's ancient history before heading to the rooftop bar and garden to unwind. How to book: Cash rates from about $227 per night or 47,000 Marriott Bonvoy points. Condesa is one of Mexico City's trendiest neighborhoods, so it only makes sense to stay in a hotel that also fits the description. At this hotel, enjoy rooftop sushi or French-Mexican fusion food; relax in the hydrotherapy pool or kick back on the patio and watch the city's cosmopolitan set roam the area. How to book: Cash rates from $339 per night or 42,000 Marriott Bonvoy points. As major hotel companies continue to expand their portfolios beyond traditional hotels, from independent boutique properties to outdoor-focused experiences, collections like Design Hotels are helping diversify what travelers can experience with points and miles. For Marriott Bonvoy members, that means more opportunities to stay somewhere truly unique without giving up the ability to earn and redeem points. And while the elite benefits might look a little different, the chance to experience a hotel with its own distinct personality might just be worth the trade-off. Related reading:

item.title: IDEA: Winter Hiking Boot FAQ
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com
If you plan to hike this winter, buy insulated, waterproof winter hiking boots to protect your feet and keep them warm. Regular hiking boots intended for three-season conditions, mids, or trail runners lack enough insulation and may not stay waterproof in wet snow, puddles, or slush. Even regular leather hiking boots treated with waterproofing products can absorb moisture, becoming cold and potentially freezing during a long outing. This can lead to discomfort, frostnip, or frostbite in severe conditions. Insulated winter hiking boots are a much better option because they have waterproof construction, rubber or waterproof synthetic lowers, and insulation that helps retain warmth even if moisture enters from above or accumulates from perspiration. While waterproof membranes such as Gore-Tex can reduce water entry, they cannot prevent dampness from sweating or the chilling effect foot perspiration can cause in cold winter weather. When that happens, insulation remains the most important factor. A damp insulated boot can still retain warmth better than an uninsulated boot that has absorbed water and begun to freeze. When choosing insulated winter hiking boots, you’ll want boots for the temperatures you expect to encounter, usually between -10°F and 35°F, although you may encounter even colder temperatures. People with cold feet may want to get more heavily insulated boots to stay warm. The temperature ratings that winter hiking boots come with assume active use, so it pays to get a boot that is even warmer if you have to stop and stand around for a while. Say, for instance, a companion is injured. You’ll want boots with enough foot insulation to stay with them until help arrives. Winter boots generally fall into three categories: Each type is designed for different conditions and activities, from winter hiking and snowshoeing to ice climbing, snowmobiling, and ice fishing. The best choice depends on how much you walk, how cold and wet the conditions are, and whether you need to use traction devices such as microspikes, snowshoes, or crampons. - Insulated waterproof winter hiking boots: These are insulated with 200g or 400g Thinsulate synthetic insulation, PrimaLoft, or Aerogel insulation and have a waterproof/breathable liner like Gore-Tex. They’re usually rated for temperatures near 0°F or lower and are single-layer boots without a removable liner. They’re good for walking and work well with microspikes or snowshoes. - Mountaineering boots: These are usually single-layer leather boots insulated with a waterproof/breathable liner made of Gore-Tex Comfort, which has added insulation. They rarely have a temperature rating and are best worn with heavier wool socks. They have very rigid soles designed for heavy crampons and aren’t easy to walk in over long distances. - Pac boots: Designed for hunting or snowmobiling, these boots are often built for frigid conditions and come with removable liners. They’re not great for walking any distance, and they don’t work well with traction aids like microspikes or crampons because their exteriors are very bulky. The waterproof/breathable liners, like Gore-Tex, built into cold-weather boots usually do a good job of keeping moisture out, especially when the boots are new. But it doesn’t hurt to add extra waterproofing, like Sno-Seal, to the outside of the boots, especially along the seams, for added protection. Waterproof/breathable liners do break down with use, and it’s good to have a backup strategy. These liners also provide poor breathability in winter, and your socks will likely get damp from perspiration if you’re active. While not ideal, this is normal, and the added insulation will keep your feet warm. If you plan to hike or snowshoe in winter, you’ll want insulated, waterproof boots designed primarily for walking, not more technical activities like mountain climbing or ice-climbing, or sedentary activities like snowmobiling or ice fishing. Winter hiking boots look like regular hiking boots, mid-height boots, or even boots with coverage above the ankle, but they’re all waterproof and insulated. For most winter hiking and snowshoeing, boots that extend just above the ankle are the most comfortable and practical. The more calf coverage you have, the warmer your feet will remain. Winter hiking boots should have laces instead of slip-on designs or zippers so you can tighten the fit. When walking on snow or ice, lug depth and rubber type matter less than your ability to use traction aids like microspikes or snowshoes, which bite into the surface and keep you from slipping. For instance, anti-slip rubber soles designed to prevent slipping on urban sidewalks are virtually worthless if you need to wear microspikes for traction most of the time. Synthetic insulated boots are usually lighter and more water-resistant than leather boots. The insulation will be built into the boot and not removable, which keeps the weight down and makes the boots easier to walk in. The amount of insulation you need depends on the temperature, how active you will be, and whether you will walk continuously or stand still for long periods. Understanding 200-Gram and 400-Gram Insulation Winter boots are commonly offered with 200-gram or 400-gram Thinsulate insulation, although PrimaLoft or Aerogel insulation is also used and provides the same level of warmth retention. The 200g and 400g quantities refer to the insulation’s thickness or density, not its weight inside your boots. As a general guide, 200-gram insulation suits active use in temperatures around 0 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit, while 400-gram insulation is better suited to temperatures between approximately -20 and -40 degrees Fahrenheit. These estimates assume that you are walking rather than standing around. Individual experiences vary considerably. We recommend the following insulated 200-gram and 400-gram winter hiking boots: Regardless of insulation level, check that your boots work properly with your microspikes, snowshoes, or crampons. Traction devices should not create excessive pressure on your toes or the front of your boots, since this can cause discomfort and blisters. This is often the case with lighter-weight winter hiking boots or mids that have soft uppers. Mountaineering boots are designed for steep, technical terrain and ice climbing. They have rigid soles that support crampons and allow climbers to stand on small edges of ice or rock. They are also generally heavier, less flexible, and less comfortable for ordinary hiking than insulated winter boots. They can also be quite bulky and may not be compatible with microspikes or even snowshoe bindings. Mountaineering boots I recommend. Mountaineering boots are available in single-layer and double-layer designs. Single-layer boots, like those listed above, are intended primarily for day trips in exposed alpine terrain. Double-layer boots have a removable liner and are best for overnight trips because you can remove a damp liner and sleep with it, preventing it from freezing overnight. They’ve largely fallen out of use, but if you’re going someplace where you need them, you can often rent them from mountain guides, especially if you’ve hired a guide service. If you need a full crampon compatible with the flexible soles of insulated winter hiking boots, look for one with a “flexible leaf spring or center bar,” like the Camp Stalker Universal Crampon. This flexible center bar connects the front spikes to the rear spike assembly. The flexible bar prevents the crampon from snapping in half when used with boots that have more flexible soles. Pac boots usually have a rubber lower section, a leather or synthetic upper, and a removable felt liner. They are designed for very cold, wet conditions, but their warmth comes with several hiking disadvantages. Pac boots are heavy, bulky, extend well above the ankle, and provide limited ankle support. They suit activities that require little walking, such as ice fishing and snowmobiling. Examples include: Their large size can also make it difficult to fit with microspikes, crampons, and most snowshoes. For active winter hiking, insulated hiking boots are usually a better choice. How Reliable Are Boot Warmth Ratings? Boot warmth ratings are useful for comparing products, but they are not standardized. Manufacturers may test their boots differently, and a rating cannot account for every person or condition. Your experience will depend on factors such as: Read customer reviews and look for boots that have been sold for several seasons. Recommendations from experienced hikers and people you trust can also be useful. Beyond insulation and waterproofing, several design details can improve comfort and performance. A manufacturer’s temperature rating provides a rough indication of warmth, but it should not be treated as a guarantee. A sturdy toe cap protects your feet and helps prevent the front of the boot from collapsing under tight-fitting microspikes or crampons. A collapsed toe box can cause pressure and blisters. A gusseted tongue is attached along its sides to the inside of the boot. It helps keep water from entering through the laces when you step into deep snow or puddles. The cuff is the upper edge of the boot around your lower leg. A soft, comfortable cuff helps retain heat and prevents snow from entering when you walk through deep snow. Deep, well-spaced lugs provide traction on packed and loose snow. Rubber compounds and tread patterns vary, but a durable sole such as Vibram can provide reliable grip. On ice, you will generally need microspikes or crampons in addition to the boot tread. A gaiter ring near the toe allows you to attach the front hook of your gaiters. If your boots do not have one, you can often attach gaiters to the laces instead. Winter boots should not be tight. A cramped boot restricts circulation and can make your feet colder. Your toes should have enough room to move, but your foot should not slide excessively from side to side. Your heel should remain secure when the boot is fully laced. Try on winter boots with the socks you plan to wear. If you wear thick winter socks, try them on during the fitting process. When between sizes, it is usually safer to choose the larger size. You can fill a small amount of extra space with thicker socks or higher-volume insoles, such as Superfeet. You can’t make a boot that’s too small larger. item.title: In Luxor, Ancient Egypt feels newly alive
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The water is cold and clear. Half-hidden amid the palm-tufted grounds of the Mortuary Temple of Seti I, this sacred sunken lake on Luxor's west bank was once the domain of ancient Egyptian priests. More than 3,000 years later, women from nearby villages still come, hoping its waters will serve as a fertility aid or a balm for their sick children, says my guide Ahmed Hassan, who was born and raised on this side of the Nile. It's one of the area's many miracles, he adds: No one knows where the water comes from, but it hasn't run dry since those priests of antiquity first bathed here. Hedging my bets, I submerge my hands. It can be difficult to know what to believe in this transcendent stretch of Upper Egypt, 410 miles south of Cairo, where the Nile exudes a life force of its own; the mountains cradle secret treasures; and the light, particularly at golden hour, plays tricks, almost convincing you that you have traveled back in time. The line between the real and the mystical feels flimsy, whether you are considering the scale of the approximately 1,000-ton, 65-foot-tall colossus of Ramses II, inexplicably carved from a single piece of granite and lying prostrate at the king's statuesque funerary temple, the Ramesseum; or observing the unnerving precision of the hieroglyphs in the tomb of Ramses V and VI, in the Valley of the Kings, that has proved immune to the ravages of time. Formerly ancient Thebes, Luxor—whose name comes from the Arabic Al-Uqsur (The Palaces)—served as Egypt's capital during the New Kingdom, from circa 1550 BCE to 1070 BCE. On the west bank of the Nile, sugarcane and banana plantations lead to a limestone canyon topped by Al-Qurn, or The Horn, a natural peak shaped like a pyramid. The rulers of the New Kingdom decided that this would be the ideal spot to protect their richly decorated tombs from grave robbers—a failed exercise, since every tomb in the Valley of the Kings was looted in antiquity, bar that of now legendary boy king Tutankhamen. “There are many sites that have an impressive amount of ‘stuff,’ but what you have in Luxor is truly monumental,” Mennat-Allah El Dorry, from the American University in Cairo's department of sociology, Egyptology, and anthropology, tells me. “You have Karnak and Luxor temples on the east bank, and the mortuary temples on the west, as well as Valley of the Kings. It is such a dense area.” I take her recommendations, balancing the quiet of the lesser-visited, only partially restored Mortuary Temple of Seti I and the Ramesseum with the many-splendored tombs at the Valley of the Kings, where voyeuristic crowds swell to see the diminutive mummy of Tutankhamen languishing 26 feet below ground. By contrast, the tomb of Ramses V and VI close by is deserted. A toothless, djellaba-wearing guard smiles conspiratorially before letting me behind the barrier. He takes my phone and assumes the practiced ease of a fashion photographer directing his next magazine cover: “Come closer; go there; look over your shoulder.” Much of Luxor feels like it hasn't changed in centuries. At sunset the sails of felucca boats trace a timeless scene on the Nile's surface. Amid the clip-clop of horse-drawn carriages, the call to prayer tumbles from minarets and the sky settles into strips of apricot and lavender. From the deck of Arax, where things do feel different, I watch night make its unhurried advance. The second offering from the homegrown Kazazian Cruises takes the motorless design of the traditional dahabeah boat and merges it with the sleek aesthetic of a luxury yacht. At every turn Nile views are given the reverence they deserve. In the airy living and dining areas, the brilliant blues and greens of the lush landscape are framed by the floor-to-ceiling glass windows of the 200-foot boat. In the nine cabins, beds clad in premium-quality Egyptian cotton face panoramic picture windows. There are Hermès toiletries, a massage therapist, and four chefs to make meals on demand. Founder Armen Kazazian identified a gap in the market for a Nile experience that offers extreme privacy and comfort on the time-honored journey between Luxor and Aswan—but also the kind of intuitive service that might see impromptu easels set up on deck to entertain the children, or a surprise beach dinner laid out on a private island. Matching the restraint of Arax is the stripped-back Marsam Hotel and discreet yet stately Habu Hotel, the latter just feet away from the Medinet Habu Temple. But Hotel Al Moudira sits at the opposite end of the spectrum. Founded by Italian Lebanese artist Zeina Aboukheir in 2001, and originally designed by famed Egyptian architect Olivier Sednaoui, the hotel revels in its maximalism: a whimsical interplay of domes and arches embellished with terra-cotta plaster, frescoes, and antiques. In 2022, Aboukheir sold the hotel to its new owner, Florian Amereller, but she still guides its creative direction, most recently in the design of six new villas. I stay in one of the five rooms in the salmon pink Villa Casbah, where hand-painted silhouettes of gazelles trip skittishly across the walls. Under its new ownership the now five-star Al Moudira has expanded to include a huge swath of surrounding farmland. It's here, in an open kitchen engulfed in greenery, that I find British Spanish chef Gioconda Scott in the midst of a busy lunch service. In 2025 she launched The Moudira Farm Kitchen, where she transforms the fresh produce grown on-site into an unfussy, seasonal menu inspired by the Mediterranean. “This is simple cooking,” says Scott, who populates her kitchen with young chefs from the local tourism college. “Every element has to be good. If you don't have a good olive oil or a good tomato, there's no hiding.” The restaurant itself is filled with products made by artisans on the farm. Crockery, rendered in a range of earthy tones, was crafted by potters whom guests can join for classes. I can hear the distant clack of the loom that wove the jaunty turquoise tablecloth, while, in other corners, artisans carve alabaster, blow glass, and upholster furniture. The same crafts inhabit the decks of Al Moudira's new, 180-foot Nile Canopus, a nostalgia-infused nod to historic travel along this evocative waterway. Open-air decks with safari-tent-style coverings, a cozy library, and rooms fitted with brass beds and bespoke teak and rattan furniture are designed to evoke the age of Amelia Edwards, author of the seminal 1877 travelogue A Thousand Miles Up the Nile. There has been a proliferation of new dahabeahs on the Nile, which offer more intimate, personalized experiences than do the hulking, 50-cabin motorboats that also ply these waters. Laden with modern conveniences, today's dahabeahs are admittedly no longer sprightly enough to be harried along by wind and sail; instead they are pushed and pulled by dinky-looking tugboats. On the inside they are increasingly elaborate. Karine Hassoun called on Egyptian painters, professors, and artisans for her eight-cabin dahabeah, Nile Divine, a celebration of contemporary Egyptian craft. In the nine-cabin Oro, a dark wood exterior pays tribute to the dahabeahs of old but with a dramatic brass wall in the reception area, a plunge pool extending out over the deck, a full-fledged bar up top, and suites with private terraces and hot tubs. Oberoi Hotels and Resorts will join the fray later this year with two seven-suite dahabeahs featuring interiors by Karim Mekhtigian, founder of Alchemy Design Studio, while Waldorf Astoria Hotels and Resorts' new, 29-suite Nile cruiser will bring to the water all the elements of its land-based hotels, including its Peacock Alley brasserie. Change is underway on land too. I see the cranes hovering over the east bank, pinpointing where a Four Seasons Hotel, due to open in 2027, is rapidly taking shape. The much-loved Winter Palace—archaeologist Howard Carter's base during his 1922 Tutankhamen tomb discovery and where Agatha Christie was inspired to write parts of Death on the Nile—recently closed for a renovation and will reopen as a Mandarin Oriental in July 2027, exactly 120 years after its official inauguration, hopefully with original features and charm fully intact. That's only weeks before next year's solar eclipse: On August 2, Luxor will witness the moon masking the sun for its maximum duration, a total of 6 minutes and 22 seconds. Just enough time for that line between the real and the mystical to grow even flimsier. A few feet from Habu Temple, recommended for its deeply etched hieroglyphs and particularly well-preserved colors, is a property with its own historic pedigree: the unassuming, 17-room Habu Hotel was one of the first hotels to open on Luxor’s West Bank in the 1920s. It has been given a smart revamp, its public areas now filled with antiques, including stately granite busts and wooden statues from the 1800s. Sundowners on the hotel’s charming rooftop terrace bring you close enough to the temple’s chiseled interior that you can admire its exterior engravings from the comfort of your lounge chair. A day spent tirelessly exploring Luxor’s sites is best ended in the spa at Hilton Luxor Resort and Spa, where treatment rooms look directly over the Nile and the infinity pool is one of the best spots in the city to catch Luxor’s famous sunsets. This is an ultra-convenient base if you want easy access to the historic sites on Luxor’s East Bank—Karnak Temple, in particular, is within walking distance. A private breakfast on a felucca offers a fresh perspective of the Nile, especially if you time it to coincide with hot-air balloons rising majestically over the Valley of the Kings. A maximalist dream on the Nile’s West Bank, Hotel Al Moudira was the first Relais and Chateaux property in Egypt. It was founded in 2001 by Italian-Lebanese artist Zeina Aboukheir, who filled it with hand-painted frescoes, antiques, artworks and furniture sourced from across Egypt. Under new ownership since 2022, the hotel offers easy access to the West Bank’s infinite sites—if you can bear to drag yourself away from its cool bougainvillea and palm-covered grounds. Six new villas offer the same, much-loved aesthetic, with a touch of extra privacy. For a stripped-back stay that’ll make you feel like an Egyptologist of old, head to Marsam Hotel, which started life as the excavation house for the University of Chicago, before being converted into a hotel in 1939. There’s (very intentionally) no swimming pool or TVs; the 29 pared-back rooms and five suites are designed for guests who are serious about exploring the many sites that surround this historic hotel. Whether or not you spend the night, make time for lunch at Marsam’s farm-to-table restaurant, where the menu changes daily and you’ll be serenaded by the resident donkeys, camels and horses.
